newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: World tea crop shortfall seen keeping prices firm.
newsitem.headline: World tea crop shortfall seen keeping prices firm.

text.p: World tea prices are seen buoyant this year because of sharp falls in production caused by drought in the biggest exporting countries of Kenya and Sri Lanka, industry officials said.
"The prices of tea are going up in (the) world market as production of the crop has been falling in major producing countries," said Hakim Khan, a tea auctioneer in Bangladesh.
The upward trend might continue if big tea producers were unable to make up the production losses over the rest of the season, he said.

Kenya, which produced a record 257 million kg of black tea in 1996, edging out Sri Lanka as the world's biggest exporter, suffered a 41 percent crop shortfall in January-April this year, leading trader Africa Tea Brokers (ATB) said.
Kenya's output fell to 54.97 million kg in January-April or 38.47 million kg below the same period in 1996, with output in April alone falling by more than half, they said.

Sri Lanka, which produced a record harvest of 258.4 million kg in 1996, had a 7.2 million kg deficit up to April this year, producing 76 million kg against 83.3 million kg in the same period of 1996, brokers John Keells said in a report.

"The crop improvement in Kenya since the onset of the rains has been relatively slow and as the start of the Indian season was also relatively poor, the international supply position in the current year is not matching up to demand," they said. "Consequently the world tea market continues to be buoyant."
Indian tea traders said firm crop estimates were not yet available but output in 1997 was expected to be around 760 million kg, against the record 780 million achieved in 1996.
India produced about 54 million kg of tea between January and March 1997, down by 4.7 million kg in the same period in 1996, they said.
Bangladesh expects lower tea output in calendar 1997 compared with 55.13 million kg in the previous year, tea market sources said.
January-April production dropped by 0.4 million kg to 5.3 million kg from the same period in 1996 in that country, they said.
Production in May-June will also be lower after a cyclone damaged tea gardens in the coastal southeastern Chittagong region, they added.
Sri Lankan brokers Forbes and Walker said Indonesia's crop in the first quarter of this year was down by three million kg to 20.6 million kg from the same period in 1996.
Africa Tea Brokers said rainfall had given way to longer periods of sunshine in key growing areas in Kenya but that temperatures remained low and growth was inhibited.
Most areas had recovered from severe drought and leaf intake was about average for the period, it said, adding that prices were higher than last year.

Lalith Ramanayake, tea director at John Keells, said Sri Lankan CTC (cut, twist, curl) teas fetched record prices earlier this year because of the dramatic shortfall in the crop in Kenya, market leader for that variety of tea.
John Keells said the Indian Ocean island's crop intakes had now improved along with the weather.

But they said earlier forecasts of cropping conditions in estates may not be realised unless the southwest monsoon, which usually sets in by mid-May and has been delayed, breaks within the next two weeks.
"During the latter part of 1996 there was a severe drought, which still appears to be continuing and could result in a shortfall in the crop," a Sri Lanka Tea Board official said.

Prices were expected to remain firm overall this year but off last year's record highs propelled by strong demand from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), the world biggest tea market, and the Middle East.
Kavi Seth of J. Thomas and Company, leading tea brokers in eastern India, said prices of Indian tea were going up this year compared to last year depending on the blend.
"Tea prices are going up because domestic consumption is increasing," said Nitin Chandra Baruah, secretary general of the Tea Association of India.
